chapter_theme: Twenty verses each count three things under one predicate (a rope to merit, a sinking mire, those called the world, the pure, husk-pounders, an army that breaks wealth), ranging from household giving and learning to statecraft and release, with a pointed attack on flesh-eating and sacrificial killing.

21.reading: Living by giving away a quarter of what comes in, the distinction of not raking over what was done when strife arose, and learning the good things after weighing many are named the excellence that good men hold to.
21.nuance: The giving is fixed as a share, கால் (a quarter) of income, not left to feeling. செருவாய்ப்பச் செய்தவை most likely means what others did to one when a quarrel arose, so the second item is forgiveness; the verse does not say whose deeds they were.

items.claim: living by giving a quarter of one's income is part of the excellence good men hold
the distinction of not searching out what was done in a quarrel is part of that excellence
learning the good after examining many things is part of that excellence

22.reading: The fetter called attachment, the chariot of craving that runs down many roads with its clinging never cut, and the hostile darkness called false speech are named three things with whose seed destroyed birth itself perishes.
22.nuance: Each fault is given an image (a rope, a runaway chariot, a darkness), and the third is a fault of speech set among two inner cravings as a cause of rebirth. The other witness reads புகையிருள் (smoky darkness) for பகையிருள், which changes the image but not the claim.

items.claim: the fetter of attachment is a seed of birth whose destruction ends birth
the chariot of craving that runs many ways unchecked is such a seed
the hostile darkness of false speech is such a seed

23.reading: The worth of giving gifts, the conduct of men of honour that has driven out faults, and a mind that has left many possessions behind are named a rope that binds good deeds for anyone.
23.nuance: கயிறு, a rope, makes the three things the means by which merit is held or drawn up; the third item is a renouncer's detachment, set beside a householder's giving as the same kind of rope.

items.claim: the worth of giving gifts is a rope to good deeds
the fault-free conduct of men of honour is such a rope
a mind that has let go of many possessions is such a rope

24.reading: The sweet words from the mouth of a courtesan with lovely soft shoulders, the frog hidden as bait inside a fishhook, and the bowing of hardened enemies are named a mire that sinks those who step in.
24.nuance: All three are pleasing surfaces over a harm: speech, bait and homage. The predicate அளறு (mire) adds that the harm is not a blow but a slow sinking.

items.claim: a courtesan's sweet speech is a mire that sinks
the frog wrapped round a hook as bait is such a mire
the bowing of hardened enemies is such a mire

25.reading: The verse reports that those who have learnt and understood do not eat from the hand of three: the petty man who lives by arrogance, the bangled woman who sells her body for a price, and the man who destroyed an endowment set apart for the good.
25.nuance: The grounds given are moral, not ritual: all three live by a wrong (pride, sale of the body, theft of a charity). அறப்புறம் is property dedicated to charity, so the third man has robbed the good themselves.

norm.note: a commensality rule of the period: whose food the learned refuse, a courtesan among them

items.claim: the learned do not eat from the hand of the petty man who lives by arrogance
they do not eat from the hand of the woman who sells her body
they do not eat from the hand of one who destroyed a charitable endowment

26.reading: The guest who knows what his host can afford, the man who lives having put away the killing of precious life, and the teacher richly possessed of sweet good conduct are named the ones who are called the world.
26.nuance: The guest is judged here, not the host: the courtesy asked of him is to know the measure of the house. ஞாலம் எனப்படுவார் means that such people are what 'the world' properly means, as உலகம் often means the worthy.

items.claim: the guest who knows the host's capacity is called the world
the man who lives refraining from killing is called the world
the teacher rich in good conduct is called the world

27.reading: Bathing before eating at mealtime, not speaking with partiality whatever one may gain, and not letting one's nobility fail even if the skin dries and one dies are named the work of those who call themselves pure.
27.nuance: The list joins a rule of bodily purity to two inner ones without ranking them; the predicate (தூஉயம் என்பார், those who say 'we are pure') makes all three the test of a claim to purity.

norm.note: a purity rule of the period: bathing before the meal

items.claim: bathing before eating is the work of those who claim purity
refusing to speak partially, whatever the gain, is such work
keeping one's nobility even unto wasting and death is such work

28.reading: The man without austerity who speaks in anger wanting to win, the man who sits craving what he does not have, and the man who listens to learning only to watch for faults are named three who pound husk and tire their hands.
28.nuance: The image of pounding husk (உமி) is labour with no grain in it: each of the three spends effort where nothing can come of it. நோன்பிலி names anger to win as a lack of austerity.

items.claim: the unrestrained man who rages to win labours for nothing
the man who sits craving what he lacks labours for nothing
the listener who only watches for faults in what is taught labours for nothing

29.reading: Not falling from one's own course even when a woman desires one and follows, having no longing for a thing even when the eye craves it and it comes to hand, and not prizing a span of life that ends in falling to the earth are named the view of the learned who sought out subtle things.
29.nuance: Each item is a restraint under the strongest temptation (the woman follows, the thing is already in hand). மண்விழுந்து வாழ்நாள் மதியாமை is hard: it may mean not counting on a life that falls to earth, or not reckoning days spent sunk in the world; the reading takes the first.

items.claim: not straying from one's course though a woman pursues one is the learned view
having no desire for a thing even when it comes to hand is the learned view
not prizing a life that ends in the earth is the learned view

30.reading: One who does not scorn those who come to him in need, one who has put away heedlessness in settled wealth, and one who has always kept clear of envy are named three whose fame endures.
30.nuance: The second item puts the danger of heedlessness in wealth that seems secure (மன்னிய செல்வம்), the moment one stops guarding it.

items.claim: one who does not scorn those who come seeking him has lasting fame
one who is not heedless in settled wealth has lasting fame
one who has always kept free of envy has lasting fame

31.reading: Learning the good among many things, carrying on without break the household life of sharing one's food, and making wealth firmly by one's own effort are named the head of all that is taught.
31.nuance: The three are learning, giving and earning, and the third supplies the second: the household shares what its own labour (தாள்) made.

items.claim: learning the good among many is the chief of all teaching
keeping household life of sharing unbroken is the chief of all teaching
making wealth by one's own effort is the chief of all teaching

32.reading: Grasping the meaning by attending to subtle words, not speaking empty words unfit for learning even when asked, and speaking good words only to those who are not base are named the debt the learned have taken on.
32.nuance: One duty of hearing and two of speaking; கடன் (debt) makes them obligations that come with learning, not graces.

items.claim: taking the meaning from subtle words is a duty of the learned
refusing to speak idle words even when asked is such a duty
speaking good words only among those who are not base is such a duty

33.reading: Subjects who live in awe of the sceptre, a minister who holds the people close like the aerial roots of a banyan, and the protection of a man firm as the bead at a spear's butt are named three that a king with an army does not let go.
33.domain_note: the king, his minister and his guard
33.nuance: The closing words படைவேந்தன் மற்று விடல் are obscure: they may mean the king must not let these go, or that a king without them is to be left; the reading takes the first. The banyan's aerial roots both hold the tree up and spread it.

items.claim: subjects who live in awe of the sceptre are what a king keeps
a minister who holds the people like banyan roots is what a king keeps
the guard of a man firm as a spear's butt-bead is what a king keeps

34.reading: The brahmin who has discharged the three debts, the king who weighs matters and does not bend justice, and the people who keep within bounds without turbulence are named the ones who are called the world.
34.domain_note: the three estates of a kingdom
34.nuance: பார்ப்பான் is a birth-group term here, defined by a ritual duty; the verse does not name the three debts, which tradition identifies as owed to sages, gods and ancestors. The verse sets priest, king and people side by side as the order that makes a 'world'.

norm.note: a varna norm of the period: the brahmin is defined by his three ritual debts

items.claim: the brahmin who has paid his three debts is called the world
the king who does not bend justice is called the world
a people that keeps within bounds without disorder is called the world

35.reading: A mind of genius that does not rise and toss like the waves of the sea, one who with great hearing of subtle texts has seen the far shore of learning, and one who without darkness of nature cuts away delusion are named three who stand on true nature.
35.nuance: மயலுறுப்பான் is read as மயல் அறுப்பான் (who cuts away delusion); taken as மயல் உறுப்பான் it would say the opposite. The first item may also mean a genius that rises above the sea's waves.

items.claim: a steady genius that does not toss like waves stands on truth
one who has reached the far shore of subtle texts stands on truth
one without dark nature who removes delusion stands on truth

36.reading: One who eats flesh and says he has compassion for living beings, one who says the killing is done without his own consent, and one who kills in a sacrifice he desires are named three who know only what they themselves have seen fit to see.
36.nuance: All three are self-justifications for taking life: a claim of compassion, a denial of complicity (the buyer who says someone else killed), and the merit of sacrifice. The closing line is ironic: their knowledge is only their own way of seeing.

norm.note: the period's dispute over flesh-eating and animal sacrifice, stated as the verse's judgment against both

items.claim: the flesh-eater who claims compassion deceives himself
one who says the killing happens without his consent deceives himself
one who kills in a sacrifice he desires deceives himself

37.reading: The measure of friendship shows in backbiting, lineage shows in a fullness of character pleasant to meet, and authority shows in a purity like milk; these three are named the way of those who hold to truth.
37.nuance: Each item is a sign by which something hidden is known. பிரமாணம் (measure, authority) and the predicate வாய்மை யடையார் வழக்கு are uncertain; அடையார் could also be negative ('those who have not attained truth'), which would reverse the predicate.

items.claim: the extent of a friendship is known by backbiting
lineage is known by pleasing fullness of character
authority is known by milk-like purity

38.reading: Admiring oneself and swelling with pride, swelling anger in vain without humility, and the meanness of coveting the many things one has set one's mind on are named an army that breaks wealth.

items.claim: self-admiring pride is an army that breaks wealth
swelling anger for nothing is such an army
the meanness of coveting many things is such an army

39.reading: Seeking the base stupor of embracing women bought with wealth, living drunk on toddy from the cup, and, scorning honest speech, bearing the stupor of lies at the dice are named the work of men without goodness.
39.nuance: Each item carries மயக்கம் (stupor), so sex for pay, drink and dice are made three kinds of intoxication. புலை here means the vile or fleshly, not a person; it is not used as a caste term.

items.claim: embracing women bought with wealth is the work of men without goodness
living drunk on toddy is such work
holding to the lies of gambling is such work

40.reading: The strength that wears anger thin, having conduct befitting toward women, and attaining the good wisdom of eating after sharing are named the work of those of ancient wisdom.
40.nuance: மகளிர்கட்கு ஒத்த லொழுக்கம் is read as a man's fitting conduct toward women (his wife); it could also be read as conduct that suits women, a rule for them. Anger is measured by quantity (நுணுக்கும், thinning), the counterpart of verse 38's swelling.

norm.note: a marital norm of the period on conduct toward women; the phrase allows more than one reading

items.claim: the strength that wears down anger is the work of the wise
having fitting conduct toward women is such work
attaining the wisdom of sharing one's food is such work

links.note: Iniyavai Narpathu calls giving with knowledge of one's income sweet; Thirikadugam fixes the share at a quarter of what comes in.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show that 'knowing one's income' had a number attached: the income is known so that a fixed fourth can go out.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam calls brooding on harm done to one smallness; Thirikadugam calls not searching out what was done in a quarrel a distinction.
links.teaches: The pair gives one act two names from both sides, and it supports reading Thirikadugam's doubtful line as forgiving injuries done to one rather than forgetting one's own deeds.

links.note: Both verses name learning the good after surveying many things and set it beside giving from the household's income.
links.teaches: The book twice pairs selective learning with measured household giving, so the pairing is a doctrine of the work and not a chance of one list.

links.note: Kural 361 calls craving the seed of unceasing birth; Thirikadugam makes craving one of three whose seed, once destroyed, ends birth.
links.teaches: The seed image is shared, but Thirikadugam widens what the seed is made of from an inner craving to include an outward act, false speech.
links.list_adds: It sets craving beside attachment and false speech, so a lie becomes one of the seeds of rebirth, which the couplet does not say.

links.note: Kural 360's triad whose end ends pain is desire, anger and confusion; Thirikadugam's triad whose end ends birth is attachment, craving and false speech.
links.teaches: Comparing the two triads shows the Kural placing the root of suffering wholly in the mind, while Thirikadugam counts a fault of speech among the roots of rebirth.
links.list_adds: It replaces anger and confusion with false speech, so the counted causes of bondage include an act of the tongue and not only states of mind.

links.note: Kural 341 says each thing one leaves removes the pain it would bring; Thirikadugam says a mind that has left many things is a rope to merit.
links.teaches: The couplet gives detachment a negative yield (pain removed); the verse gives it a positive one (merit bound), so letting go both frees and gains.
links.list_adds: It sets the detached mind beside the gift and honourable conduct, so the renouncer's letting go and the householder's giving are one kind of rope.

links.note: Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who want wealth, not love, bring harm; Thirikadugam names a courtesan's sweet speech a sinking mire.
links.teaches: Kural names the harm; the verse names the mechanism, a pleasing surface over a hook, and its effect, a slow sinking rather than a blow.
links.list_adds: It groups the courtesan's speech with bait on a hook and an enemy's bowing, so it becomes one of three lures whose sweetness hides the danger.

links.note: Both use the fishhook: Kural 931 likens gambling winnings to the hook a fish swallows; Thirikadugam names the frog wrapped round a hook as bait.
links.teaches: The ethics group uses the hook for any pleasure that is the means of capture: the Kural shows it from inside the fish after the gain, Thirikadugam at the bait before it.
links.list_adds: It turns the hook from an image of gambling gains into one of three snares beside flattery by a courtesan and by a foe.

links.note: Kural 828 says a weapon hides in an enemy's folded hands; Thirikadugam calls the bowing of hardened enemies a mire.
links.teaches: The couplet names what the homage hides, a weapon, and the verse what it does to the one who trusts it: he sinks.
links.list_adds: It puts an enemy's homage beside a courtesan's sweet words, so political and sexual flattery are reckoned one kind of trap.

links.note: Kural 915 says those of refined understanding do not plunge into the charms of common women; Thirikadugam says the learned do not eat from such a woman's hand.
links.teaches: The Kural's avoidance is of her body; the verse's is of her food, so the learned man's refusal reaches even to accepting maintenance from her.
links.list_adds: It groups her with the arrogant petty man and the robber of a charity, so the bar falls on all who live by a wrong means, not on sex alone.

links.note: Both close by naming three who are called the world: verse 26 a considerate guest, a non-killer and a gentle teacher; verse 34 the brahmin, the just king and orderly people.
links.teaches: The book defines 'the world' twice, once by three private virtues and once by three estates, so the word means both good persons and an ordered society.

links.note: Kural 325 makes the one who refrains from killing the chief of all renouncers; Thirikadugam counts him among those who are the world.
links.teaches: The Kural honours non-killing at the head of renunciation; the verse honours it in ordinary social life, so it is a summit in both ways of living.
links.list_adds: It sets the non-killer beside a considerate guest and a teacher of good conduct, taking non-killing out of the renouncers' ranking into everyday company.

links.note: Kural 113 says to let go at once of gain that leaves fairness, even if it brings good; Thirikadugam counts not speaking partially, whatever one gains, as the work of the pure.
links.teaches: The Kural sets fairness against gain; the verse calls the same refusal a purity, so impartial speech is a cleanliness and not only a justice.
links.list_adds: It makes impartiality one of three purities with bathing before meals and nobility unto death, joining a bodily rite to two inner virtues.

links.note: Kural 298 divides outer purity, made by water, from inner purity, seen in truth; Thirikadugam lists bathing before meals with impartial speech and unfailing nobility as the work of the pure.
links.teaches: The couplet separates the two purities; the verse joins them in one list and implies that a claim to purity needs both at once.
links.list_adds: It counts the water-purity and two inner purities as one work without ranking them, where the couplet ranks them by kind.

links.note: Iniyavai Narpathu calls sweet the austerity of one who wants to win and does not rage, and not craving what one lacks; Thirikadugam says the one without austerity who rages to win and the one who craves what he lacks pound husk.
links.teaches: The two works state the same pair from opposite sides in nearly the same words, so restraint in contest and in craving is both a sweetness and the only labour that bears grain.

links.note: Iniyavai Narpathu calls sweet not snatching what one sees and desires; Thirikadugam asks for no desire for a thing even once it is in one's hand.
links.teaches: The pair grades the restraint: not seizing what is seen is the lower step, not wanting what is already held is the higher.

links.note: Kural 532 says heedlessness kills fame as chronic want kills understanding; Thirikadugam says one who has put away heedlessness in settled wealth keeps lasting fame.
links.teaches: The couplet states the threat to fame in general; the verse says when it strikes, when wealth seems secure.
links.list_adds: It places the vigilant rich man beside the courteous giver and the man free of envy, so fame rests on three habits of the wealthy.

links.note: Kural 1057 tells of the seeker's joy at givers who do not scorn; Thirikadugam gives lasting fame to the man who does not scorn those who seek him.
links.teaches: The same courtesy pays both parties: the seeker gets inner joy and the giver lasting renown.
links.list_adds: It turns the seeker's joy into the giver's renown and ranks the courtesy with vigilance and freedom from envy.

links.note: Kural 322 crowns sharing food and sustaining life as the head of all the authors gathered; Thirikadugam crowns three things as the head of all that is heard: selective learning, unbroken sharing household life, and making wealth by effort.
links.teaches: Sharing food is the head in both, but Thirikadugam shares the crown with the learning that guides the giving and the earning that supplies it.
links.list_adds: It divides the couplet's single crown among three, adding learning and self-made wealth to the act of sharing.

links.note: Kural 424 defines understanding partly as seeing the subtle meaning in others' words; Thirikadugam makes taking the meaning from subtle words a debt the learned owe.
links.teaches: The couplet describes a capacity; the verse turns it into an obligation that comes with learning.
links.list_adds: It joins the duty of subtle hearing to two duties of speech, silence when idle words are asked for and speech only to the not-base.

links.note: Naladiyar 197 says a son props a failing father as aerial roots hold up a termite-eaten banyan; Thirikadugam says a good minister holds the people like the banyan's aerial roots.
links.teaches: The same image of support from below serves the family and the state: the minister is to the kingdom what a son is to an ageing father.
links.list_adds: It sets the root-like minister between the sceptre-fearing people and the firm guard as one of a king's three supports.

links.note: Kural 542 says the people live looking to the king's sceptre as the world looks to rain; Thirikadugam names people who live in awe of the sceptre as a support of the king.
links.teaches: The sceptre has two faces to the people, hope in the Kural and fear in Thirikadugam, and the verse counts that fear as an asset of rule.
links.list_adds: It makes the subjects' awe of the rod one of three things a king keeps, with a minister and a guard.

links.note: Kural 560 says the six-duty brahmins forget their texts when the king fails to guard; Thirikadugam sets the brahmin who has paid his debts beside the just king and orderly people as the world.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the brahmin's ritual learning depend on good rule; the verse makes it a coordinate pillar beside the king.
links.list_adds: It lists priest, king and people as three parts of one order rather than as cause and effect.

links.note: Kural 541 defines justice as investigating (ஓர்ந்து), showing no favour and acting after consideration; Thirikadugam names the king who weighs matters (ஓர்ந்து) and does not bend justice.
links.teaches: Both put weighing first in justice, but the verse makes the just king only one third of what makes a world.
links.list_adds: It places the just king between the dutiful brahmin and the orderly people, so justice is one estate's part of a shared order.

links.note: Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore and life is short; Thirikadugam praises one who has seen the shore of the texts.
links.teaches: Read together, mastering a body of texts (நூல்) is possible while learning (கல்வி) itself has no end, so the two claims are about different things.
links.list_adds: It ranks the one who reached the texts' shore with a steady mind and freedom from delusion as three who stand on truth.

links.note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh if the world did not kill to eat; Thirikadugam names the man who says the killing happens without his consent as self-deceived.
links.teaches: The verse names the buyer's excuse in his own words, and the couplet supplies the answer: the purchase is the cause.
links.list_adds: It puts the eater who disclaims the killing beside the flesh-eater who claims compassion and the sacrificer, so three justifications are one kind.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 says the one who consented, the buyer, the cook and the eater share the killer's sin; Thirikadugam mocks one who says the deed is done without his consent.
links.teaches: Both answer the disclaimer by spreading guilt along the chain: Sirupanchamoolam lists the chain, Thirikadugam ridicules the man who denies his link in it.

links.note: Kural 259 ranks not killing to eat above a thousand sacrifices; Thirikadugam names one who kills in a desired sacrifice as one who knows only his own view.
links.teaches: The Kural weighs sacrifice against abstention; the verse drops the weighing and calls ritual killing a self-deception.
links.list_adds: It groups the sacrificer with two flesh-eaters, so ritual killing is reckoned with ordinary meat-eating rather than above it.

links.note: Kural 188 asks what those who spread the faults of their intimates will do to strangers; Thirikadugam says the measure of friendship shows in backbiting.
links.teaches: The couplet reasons from near to far; the verse makes backbiting the gauge by which one learns how far a friendship really reaches.
links.list_adds: It sets backbiting as a test of friendship beside tests of lineage and of authority, three signs by which hidden worth is known.

links.note: Kural 431 says the prosperity of those without arrogance, anger and smallness is dignified; Thirikadugam names arrogance, anger and the smallness of coveting as an army that breaks wealth.
links.teaches: The same triad is the condition of wealth's dignity when absent and the force that destroys wealth when present.
links.list_adds: It turns the couplet's three absent faults into one hostile army and defines the third, smallness, as coveting many things.

links.note: Verse 38 makes swelling anger part of an army that breaks wealth; verse 40 makes the strength that wears anger thin the work of the wise.
links.teaches: The book measures anger by quantity, swelling or thinning, and ties the first to lost wealth and the second to old wisdom.

links.note: Kural 920 names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left; Thirikadugam names the same three as the work of men without goodness.
links.teaches: Both name the same three vices, and the verse adds what they share: each is a stupor (மயக்கம்).
links.list_adds: It calls each item a மயக்கம், so paid sex and dice are made forms of intoxication alongside drink.

links.note: Kural 913 likens the false embrace of women bought with wealth to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; Thirikadugam calls it seeking a base stupor (புலைமயக்கம்).
links.teaches: The couplet's corpse and the verse's புலை both make the bought embrace a contact with something vile, one by image, one by name.
links.list_adds: It sets the bought embrace in a series of three stupors with drink and dice.

links.note: Kural 310 says those who renounce anger equal those who renounce all; Thirikadugam names the strength that wears anger thin as the work of the anciently wise beside household duties.
links.teaches: The Kural lifts quelling anger to the level of renunciation; the verse keeps it as a householder's strength (விறல்).
links.list_adds: It places anger's control with conduct toward women and sharing food, so it is counted among household virtues rather than set equal to renunciation.

26: the verse is printed without a number in the source and numbered 26 by its place.
36 line 1: the other witness reads அருளுடையெம் for அருளுடையேம்.
39 line 3: சூதின் கண்தாங்கால் looks like a misprint for சூதின்கண் தாங்கல், the verbal noun the other items have.
40 line 1: விறலு மகளிர்கட்கு splits விறலும் across the word break.
33 line 4: படைவேந்தன் மற்று விடல் is obscure and may be corrupt.
